documents: Ji, Wang, Hofmann, Kwiatek & Dresen (2022), High-rate fluid injection reduces the nucleation length of laboratory earthquakes on critically stressed faults in granite, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL100418 (published PDF, 13 pp.; Supporting Information not supplied)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (n of 13); references to Supporting Information items are given as the main-text page plus the SI item (e.g. '3 (Text S1)') because the supplement was not supplied

entry.evidence: a systematic laboratory study characterizing the injection-rate dependence of earthquake nucleation length of faults in rock samples and its implications for injection-induced seismicity are lacking.

sequences.source_document: Ji et al. 2022, GRL, published PDF

steps.action: The authors take from rate-and-state theory and earlier dry-sample experiments the expectation that nucleation length decreases with higher normal stress and higher loading rate.
steps.quote: the directly measured nucleation length for dry samples is found to decrease with higher normal stress

steps.action: The authors adopt Gori et al.'s (2021) suggestion from polymer experiments that high-rate injection acts as dynamic loading and shrinks nucleation length.
steps.quote: suggesting that higher injection rates may constitute dynamic loading and reduce the [...]

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how injection-induced nucleation length depends on local injection rate and effective stress on critically stressed faults in granite.
steps.quote: a systematic laboratory study characterizing the injection-rate dependence of earthquake nucleation length of faults in rock samples

steps.action: The authors design triaxial injection tests on 30° sawcut low-permeability Odenwald granite with a borehole to the fault, six fault-parallel strain gauges, eight PZT pairs for AE location (AIC plus CNN picking, layered anisotropic velocity model), and two injection rates and two confining pressures.
steps.quote: we injected fluid locally through a small borehole to critically stressed sawcut faults in low-permeability granite samples at different injection rates and confining pressures

steps.action: In an additional series, the authors moved the strain gauges to alternative locations to check the constraint on nucleation length (reported in the supplement).
steps.quote: In the additional series of experiments, we used alternative locations of strain gauges to constrain the nucleation length

steps.action: The authors set the conditions on one sample in sequence (S1-1: 0.2 mL/min at 31 MPa; S1-2: 0.8 mL/min at 31 MPa; S1-3: 0.8 mL/min at 61 MPa, all at 85% of peak strength) and ran a second series S2 at 90% on another sample.
steps.quote: A second fluid injection experiment S1-2 (Figure 2b) was conducted on the same sample at a higher injection rate of 0.8 mL/min

steps.action: From the injection and monitoring pressures, the authors estimate the spatio-temporal fluid pressure distribution on the fault with a finite element model, and quantify its heterogeneity as a standard deviation.
steps.quote: estimate the spatial-temporal evolution of fluid pressure on the fault surface using a finite element model

steps.action: The authors observe mostly stick-slip events, with two slow slip events, during injection. Fault stiffness exceeds system stiffness for stick-slip, consistent with Rice/Ruina stability theory. Peak slip rates are larger at higher injection rate and confining pressure.
steps.quote: during the injection stage, we observed mostly stick-slip events (i.e., laboratory earthquakes exhibiting sudden macroscopic fault slip)

steps.action: The authors record AE activity: very few events at 31 MPa, abundant events at 61 MPa, and larger AE increases for higher-rate injections.
steps.quote: Fault slip induced by fluid injection produced very limited AE activity (cumulative AE number < 20) at 31 MPa confining pressure

steps.action: The authors infer the average friction coefficient from average shear stress and model-derived average effective normal stress. It is Byerlee-like (0.5-0.8) at 31 MPa but drops strongly at 61 MPa.
steps.quote: the average friction coefficient at 61 MPa reduced dramatically to ∼0.07 and ∼0.3

steps.action: The authors convert local axial strains to local shear stress (constant Young's modulus) and estimate bounded dimensionless nucleation lengths Lc(sg)/Lf from the extent of premonitory stress drops along the gauge array. Values are 0.71-1 at 0.2 mL/min and 0.29-0.43 at 0.8 mL/min, with a contained rupture (≤0.15) at 61 MPa.
steps.quote: the local axial strain change was converted to local shear stress change (Passelègue et al., 2016, 2020) assuming a constant Young's modulus

steps.action: The authors replicate the observations on a second sample (series S2 at 90% peak strength), including a second contained rupture in S2-3.
steps.quote: A similar contained rupture was again observed in the third experiment S2-3

steps.action: The authors cross-check strain-gauge nucleation lengths against nucleation lengths from the 2D spreading of AE clusters (reported in the supplement).
steps.quote: Our estimates of dimensionless nucleation lengths determined by the strain gauge data are supported by results obtained from 2D spreading of AE clusters

steps.action: The authors examine the fault surfaces after testing and find reduced asperity height and melt structures. They propose powder lubrication and melting/thermal pressurization as weakening mechanisms at 61 MPa.
steps.quote: the root mean square asperity height was reduced by 20 μm, suggesting asperity damage after the experiments

steps.action: The authors compile all experiments, excluding most 61 MPa results because of friction loss but keeping the two contained ruptures. They show Lc/Lf falls with effective normal stress and compare this with theory and prior experiments.
steps.quote: decreases significantly from ∼0.9 to <0.15 as average effective normal stress increases from ∼19 to ∼87 MPa

steps.action: The authors normalize nucleation length by effective normal stress and show it decreases from 0.2 to 0.8 mL/min, similar to loading-rate effects in displacement-driven experiments.
steps.quote: reduces significantly with higher injection rate (Figure 4b)

steps.action: The authors propose that fluid-pressure heterogeneity, which correlates with smaller nucleation length, makes nucleation occur over smaller patches, possibly via spatio-temporally varying rate-and-state parameters.
steps.quote: it is conceivable that the stress heterogeneity caused by local fluid pressure perturbation may have caused nucleation of injection-induced laboratory earthquakes over smaller fault patches

steps.action: The authors compute the theoretical quasistatic (Lb−a) and minimum dynamic (Lb) nucleation lengths from literature rate-and-state parameters for bare granite, giving about 78.3 and 11.2 MPa normalized.
steps.quote: We also compare the measured nucleation length with theoretical predictions.

steps.action: The authors compare measured normalized nucleation lengths (6.5-37.0 MPa) with the theoretical bounds and find agreement within an order of magnitude.
steps.quote: Our laboratory measurements of nucleation lengths using strain gauges agree with theoretical predictions within one order of magnitude.

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that nucleation length shrinks with higher injection rate and effective normal stress, and draw implications for injection-induced seismic hazard.
steps.quote: nucleation lengths of injection-induced stick-slip events along sawcut faults in granite reduce with higher effective normal stress and higher injection rate

tree.answer: Injection-induced laboratory earthquakes and their nucleation length on sawcut granite faults
No; nucleation length inferred from strain-gauge stress changes (and AE spreading)
Dependence of nucleation length on injection rate and effective normal stress
No stated rivals; one cited expectation (dynamic loading shrinks nucleation length)
Rate-and-state theory gives quasistatic and dynamic bounds; only an order-of-magnitude comparison
Set in the lab: injection rate, confining pressure, initial shear stress
Partly: second sample series, AE cross-check, alternative gauge positions; most 61 MPa data excluded
Nucleation length shrinks with higher injection rate and effective normal stress

end.claim: On critically stressed sawcut faults in low-permeability granite, the nucleation length of injection-induced laboratory earthquakes decreases with higher injection rate (0.2 to 0.8 mL/min) and higher effective normal stress (about 19 to 87 MPa), within experimental uncertainties.

decisive_move.sentence: Estimating bounded nucleation lengths from the premonitory local shear-stress drops along the six-gauge strain array is what produces the quantity whose rate and stress dependence is claimed.

gates.evidence: Action: the cited dynamic-loading suggestion (Gori et al. 2021) and rate-and-state expectations motivated varying the injection rate, but the aim is framed as exploring the dependence (p. 2). Claim: the trend could have failed to appear. However, there are only two injection rates and two samples, the 61 MPa data were mostly excluded after the fact (p. 9), and the theory comparison is only order-of-magnitude (p. 10). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: convolutional neural network for refining P-wave onset picks (after Ross et al. 2018)
Akaike Information Criterion picker for rough P-wave onsets
grid search followed by simplex optimization for hypocenter inversion
Savitzky-Golay filter for removing high-frequency strain-gauge noise
finite element model of fluid pressure diffusion on the fault
strain gauges for local strain and stress measurement
density-based clustering (Ester et al. 1996), cited in the Supporting Information references, presumably for AE clusters (inference)

novelty_claims.quote: This study systematically demonstrates that higher injection rates constitute dynamic loading, which increase the seismic hazard by shrinking the earthquake nucleation length.
A smaller nucleation length associated with larger injection rates at higher effective normal stresses has been systematically observed

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: higher peak slip rates and larger slip displacements for smaller nucleation lengths are an observed association (regularity_in_range, p. 10-11). The role of fluid-pressure heterogeneity is a conjecture without status (p. 10). Smaller patches slipping seismically at higher rates in the field is an implication only (p. 10). The paper does not show: (1) the Supporting Information, which was not supplied, so the checks in Texts S1, S5, S6 and Figures S9-S14 are coded from main-text statements only; (2) a review file, though the acknowledgments mention editor and referee reviews, so no review sequence could be coded; (3) whether the exclusion rule for 61 MPa data was set before seeing the nucleation results (inference: post hoc, justified by the friction drop); (4) any statistical fit or uncertainty beyond the gauge-spacing bounds. The injection-rate dependence rests on two rates on two samples, with repeated reuse of the same sample, so slip hardening and history may confound rate (the paper notes hardening between S1-1 and S1-2, p. 5). Peak slip rates are likely underestimated at 5,120 Hz sampling (p. 6). Rupture velocities are apparent values because of the mixed-mode 2D geometry (p. 8).

disagreements.target: Two-stage nucleation (quasi-static then accelerating) described by Ohnaka & Shen (1999) and Latour et al. (2013)
disagreements.support: The two phases were not resolved at 31 MPa; the authors attribute this to mixed-mode rupture on their elliptical fault rather than to the long, narrow mode II faults used previously.
disagreements.quote: were not well resolved by the strain gauge array before the injection-induced dynamic slip events at 31 MPa confining pressure

disagreements.target: Injected fluid volume as the control on induced seismicity (McGarr, 2014; McGarr & Barbour, 2018)
disagreements.support: Measured shrinkage of nucleation length with injection rate suggests that rate, not only volume, regulates seismic hazard.
disagreements.quote: Our results thus highlight the role of injection rate on regulating injection-induced seismicity in addition to injected fluid volume

disagreements.support: Average friction at 61 MPa fell to about 0.07-0.3 with slip, which the authors attribute to additional weakening (asperity damage, possible powder lubrication, melt structures).

alternatives_considered.chosen: Nucleation length from strain-gauge premonitory stress drops
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Nucleation length from precursory AE hypocenter locations (2D spreading of AE clusters)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Project the 2D elliptical fault onto a 1D fault length of 100 mm along the slip direction
alternatives_considered.reason: in order to estimate the nucleation length

alternatives_considered.chosen: Constant Young's modulus of the rock matrix to convert strain to shear stress
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Accounting for transient confining-pressure changes during slip
alternatives_considered.reason: high compliance of the confining system makes transient changes minor

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exclude most 61 MPa results, keeping the two contained ruptures
alternatives_considered.reason: significant drop of average friction coefficient at 61 MPa with continuing slip

alternatives_considered.chosen: Normalized nucleation length (σn−p)Lc/Lf plotted against injection rate
alternatives_considered.reason: inverse dependence of nucleation length on effective normal stress
